meanings.short: The value a quantity gets closer and closer to, as near as we like, as its input approaches some value, without having to reach it.
meanings.long: We write lim f(x) as x → a. The limit may exist even where f itself is not defined, as sin x / x does at x = 0, where its limit is 1. Derivatives, integrals and the sums of infinite series are all defined as limits; physicists also speak of the classical or Newtonian limit, the regime a theory approaches.

meanings.short: A bound: the largest or smallest possible or allowed value, such as the most mass a white dwarf can have.
meanings.long: Physicists speak of the Chandrasekhar limit, the Eddington limit or the resolution limit of a telescope. A measurement often gives only an upper or lower limit on a quantity.

meanings.short: In an integral, one of the two end values between which it is taken, the lower or upper limit of integration.
meanings.long: In the integral from a to b, the numbers a and b are the limits of integration. They are not limits in the sense of a value approached.

everyday: In everyday speech a limit is a maximum, as in a speed limit; in calculus it is the value a quantity approaches.

meanings.short: The two end values, lower and upper, between which a definite integral is taken: the a and b in the integral from a to b.
meanings.long: Changing the variable of integration changes the limits too: they must be rewritten in terms of the new variable. Swapping the two limits changes the sign of the integral.

meanings.short: Without breaks, gaps or jumps: a continuous graph can be drawn without lifting the pen; a continuous quantity can take every value in a range.
meanings.long: A function f is continuous at a point a when its limit there equals its value, lim f(x) = f(a) as x → a. In physics a continuous quantity or spectrum can take every value in a range, not only separate ones.

meanings.short: Of a phase transition: with no sudden jump in energy or volume (no latent heat), though some derivative changes sharply.
A point where a function is not continuous: its graph jumps, has a hole or shoots off to infinity there.
meanings.long: The main kinds are removable discontinuities (a hole that could be filled), jump discontinuities and infinite discontinuities. A function can also be discontinuous by wiggling ever faster, as sin(1/x) does near 0.

meanings.short: A point where a graph jumps: the function has a limit from the left and a limit from the right, but they differ.
meanings.long: A step function, which is 0 for negative x and 1 for positive x, has a jump discontinuity at 0. Its graph is two separate pieces at different heights.

meanings.short: A hole in a graph: the limit exists, but the function is undefined there or has a different value, so redefining one point repairs it.
meanings.long: sin x / x is undefined at 0, but its limit there is 1; setting the value at 0 to 1 makes the function continuous. The name says it: one value can remove the problem.

meanings.short: A point where a function shoots off to plus or minus infinity, as 1/x does at x = 0.
meanings.long: The graph has a vertical asymptote there. The two sides may go to the same infinity or, as for 1/x, to opposite ones.

meanings.short: Having a derivative: at that point the graph has a single, definite, non-vertical tangent line, with no corner or break.
meanings.long: A differentiable function is always continuous, but not the other way round: |x| is continuous at 0 but has a corner there, so it is not differentiable at 0. Most functions met in physics are differentiable except at a few special points.

meanings.short: Finding a derivative: working out how fast a function changes.
meanings.long: Rules such as the product, quotient and chain rules turn differentiation into a routine calculation. Integration undoes it, up to a constant.

meanings.short: The change in a function divided by the change in its input, the slope of a secant line: [f(x + Δx) − f(x)]/Δx.
meanings.long: Its limit as Δx goes to zero is the derivative. Computers estimate derivatives with difference quotients for small Δx.

meanings.short: How fast one quantity changes compared with another, often time: the change in the first divided by the change in the second.
meanings.long: The average rate of change over an interval is a difference quotient; the instantaneous rate of change at a point is the derivative. Speed is the rate of change of distance with time.

meanings.short: The rule that the derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹; read backwards, it integrates powers of x.
meanings.long: It holds for every real power n. Run in reverse it gives ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, which fails only for n = −1, whose integral is the logarithm.

meanings.short: The rule for the derivative of a fraction of two functions: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v².
meanings.long: It follows from the product rule and the chain rule applied to u times 1/v. For example (sin x / x)′ = (x cos x − sin x)/x².

meanings.short: Finding dy/dx from an equation that links x and y, by differentiating both sides and solving for dy/dx, without first solving for y.
meanings.long: For the circle x² + y² = 1, differentiating gives 2x + 2y y′ = 0, so y′ = −x/y. It also gives the derivatives of inverse functions such as the arcsine.

meanings.short: Of a function: given by an equation linking x and y, such as x² + y² = 1, not by a formula y = f(x).
Of a function or equation: solved for the unknown, written as a formula y = f(x) that gives y directly.
Finding a derivative by first taking the natural logarithm of the function, which turns products and powers into sums.
meanings.long: It handles functions such as xˣ, where the variable is in both base and exponent: ln y = x ln x, so y′/y = ln x + 1. It also simplifies long products and quotients before differentiating.

meanings.short: The derivative of ln f, equal to f′/f: the rate of change of a quantity as a fraction of its size.
meanings.long: It is also called the relative rate. A population growing 2 per cent a year has a relative rate of 0.02 per year whatever its size; the Hubble rate ȧ/a is the relative rate of growth of the universe.

meanings.short: The product of all the whole numbers from 1 up to n, written n!; for example 4! = 24.
meanings.long: 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24, and by convention 0! = 1. Factorials grow faster than any power, and n! counts the ways to put n things in order.

meanings.short: The formula for multiplying out a power of a sum, (a + b)ⁿ, as a sum of terms with known whole-number coefficients.
meanings.long: (a + b)ⁿ = aⁿ + n aⁿ⁻¹ b + n(n − 1)/2 aⁿ⁻² b² + … + bⁿ. For powers that are not whole numbers it becomes an infinite series, (1 + x)ᵃ = 1 + ax + …, useful when x is small.

meanings.short: Doing one function and then another to its result, as in sin(x²): the inner function's output is the outer function's input.
meanings.long: The composition of f and g is written f(g(x)) or f ∘ g. Its derivative is given by the chain rule.

meanings.short: The function that undoes another: if f turns x into y, its inverse turns y back into x.
meanings.long: Its graph is the graph of f reflected in the line y = x. The logarithm is the inverse of the exponential, and the arcsine the inverse of the sine on a chosen range.

meanings.short: The natural unit of angle: the angle whose arc on a circle is as long as the radius. A full turn is 2π radians.
meanings.long: One radian is about 57.3 degrees. Calculus formulas such as (sin x)′ = cos x hold only when angles are in radians, and an arc of angle θ has length rθ.

meanings.short: The circle of radius 1 centred at the origin; the point at angle θ on it is (cos θ, sin θ).
meanings.long: It defines sine and cosine for every angle, and the length of its arc from angle 0 to angle θ is θ itself, in radians. Going once round it is a turn of 2π radians.

meanings.short: A point where a function's derivative is zero, so its graph is level there; maxima and minima are found among such points.
meanings.long: At a critical point x₀, f′(x₀) = 0. It may be a maximum, a minimum or neither (as for x³ at 0). For a function of several variables all the partial derivatives are zero there.

meanings.short: A constant solution of an equation such as dy/dt = f(y): a value where the rate of change is zero, also called an equilibrium.
meanings.long: If y starts at a critical point it stays there. Nearby solutions move towards a stable critical point and away from an unstable one.

meanings.short: The temperature and pressure above which liquid and gas can no longer be told apart.
meanings.long: Below it a liquid and its vapour can sit side by side with a sharp boundary; at the critical point that difference vanishes and quantities such as the compressibility grow without limit.

meanings.short: The amount of damping at which an oscillator just stops oscillating, called critical damping.
meanings.long: With less damping the system oscillates as it settles; with more it creeps back slowly. Critical damping returns it fastest without overshooting.

meanings.short: The value a function takes at a critical point.
meanings.long: If x₀ is a critical point of f, then f(x₀) is a critical value. The largest and smallest values of a function on an interval are among its critical values and its values at the ends.

meanings.short: A point where a graph changes the way it bends, from bending up to bending down or the other way.
meanings.long: There the second derivative changes sign. The graph of x³ has an inflection point at 0; the graph of the sine has one wherever it crosses the axis.

meanings.short: Of a graph: bending, either upwards like a cup (concave up) or downwards like a cap (concave down).
meanings.long: A graph is concave up where its second derivative is positive, so its slope increases, and concave down where the second derivative is negative. A ball rolling on a concave-up curve sits at its lowest point in stable equilibrium.

meanings.short: A straight line that a graph gets closer and closer to, without reaching it, as the graph heads off to infinity.
meanings.long: y = 1/x has the x-axis as a horizontal asymptote and the y-axis as a vertical one. A function behaves asymptotically like another when their ratio tends to 1.

meanings.short: A way to sort a critical point: if the second derivative there is positive it is a minimum; if negative, a maximum.
meanings.long: If the second derivative is zero the test says nothing, and the point must be studied in another way. With several variables a version of the test uses all the second partial derivatives.

meanings.short: Problems in which several quantities change together, and differentiating the equation that links them links their rates of change.
meanings.long: If a ladder slides down a wall, x² + y² = L² gives x x′ + y y′ = 0, so the speed of its foot fixes the speed of its top. The trick is to differentiate the equation that links the quantities before putting in numbers.

meanings.short: A way to solve f(x) = 0: make a guess, follow the tangent line to where it crosses zero, and repeat from there.
meanings.long: Each step replaces x by x − f(x)/f′(x). Near a simple root the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step, but a bad first guess can send it to the wrong root or nowhere.

meanings.short: If a function is smooth between two points, somewhere between them its slope equals its average slope over the whole interval.
meanings.long: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable inside, there is a c between a and b with f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a). In motion: at some moment your speed equals your average speed.

meanings.short: A statement that has been proved true, step by step, from definitions and earlier results.
meanings.long: A theorem lists its conditions (hypotheses) and its conclusion; if a condition is dropped, the conclusion may fail. Smaller theorems used along the way are called lemmas.

everyday: In everyday speech proof means strong evidence; a mathematical proof shows that a statement holds in every case, with no exceptions.

meanings.short: A chain of reasoning showing beyond doubt that a statement follows from definitions and results already known.
meanings.long: Each step must follow from the ones before. Checking many examples is not a proof; a single counterexample is enough to disprove a statement.

meanings.short: Producing a voltage, and so a current, in a circuit by changing the magnetic field through it, as in a generator or transformer.
meanings.long: Faraday discovered it in 1831. The induced voltage equals minus the rate of change of the magnetic flux through the circuit.

meanings.short: A way to prove a statement for every whole number n: prove it for n = 1, then show that each case implies the next.
meanings.long: Like a row of dominoes: the first falls, and each one knocks over the next, so all of them fall. It is used to prove formulas such as the nth derivative of xⁿ being n!.

meanings.short: A way to prove a statement for every whole number n: prove it for n = 1, then show that each case implies the next.
Charging a body without touching it, by bringing a charged object near so that the body's own charges separate.
Reasoning from many particular cases, such as a few springs tested, to a general law that is then trusted for all cases.
A rule that acts on a function, vector or state and turns it into another one, such as 'take the derivative'.
meanings.long: The derivative d/dx is an operator: it turns sin x into cos x. In quantum mechanics every measurable quantity, such as momentum or energy, is represented by an operator acting on the state.

meanings.short: In quantum physics, an operator that removes one quantum of energy, or one particle, from a state.
meanings.long: For the harmonic oscillator it lowers the energy by one step ħω, and acting on the ground state it gives zero. Its partner, the creation operator, adds a quantum.

meanings.short: How fast the universe expands: the rate at which distances between galaxies grow, as a fraction of their size, per unit of time.
meanings.long: It is H = ȧ/a, with a the scale factor. Today's value is the Hubble constant H₀, about 70 km/s per megaparsec: galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance, with H as the factor.

meanings.short: A growth by a factor of e, about 2.718; the number of e-folds in a growth is the natural logarithm of the total factor.
meanings.long: Growing a million times takes ln(10⁶), about 14 e-folds. Inflation is usually said to need at least about 60 e-folds of expansion.

meanings.short: The rule that turns small changes of coordinates into real distances or time intervals, and so sets the geometry of a space or spacetime.
meanings.long: It is usually written as a formula for ds², such as ds² = dx² + dy² for a flat plane. Curved surfaces, the expanding universe and black holes each have their own metric; in general relativity the metric describes gravity.

everyday: Not the metric system of units: here a metric is a rule for measuring distance.

origin: Greek logos, ratio, and arithmos, number.

meanings.short: The power to which a fixed base must be raised to give a number: log₁₀ 1000 = 3 because 10³ = 1000.
meanings.long: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition: log(xy) = log x + log y. A logarithmic scale gives equal steps to equal ratios, as the magnitude scale and decibels do.

meanings.short: The logarithm to base e, about 2.718, written ln x: the power to which e must be raised to give x.
meanings.long: It is the area under 1/t from 1 to x, and its derivative is 1/x, which is why it appears whenever something grows at a rate proportional to its size. ln e = 1 and ln 1 = 0.

meanings.short: Cousins of sine and cosine built from exponentials: sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, and their ratios.
meanings.long: They satisfy cosh² x − sinh² x = 1, as the points (cosh t, sinh t) lie on a hyperbola. A hanging chain takes the shape of a cosh curve, and tanh x = sinh x / cosh x appears in magnetisation and relativity.

meanings.short: A function whose derivative is the given function; any two antiderivatives differ only by a constant.
meanings.long: x³/3 is an antiderivative of x², and so is x³/3 + 5. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, definite integrals are differences of antiderivatives.

meanings.short: The family of all antiderivatives of a function, written ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + c with an arbitrary constant c.
meanings.long: It has no limits of integration and gives a function, not a number. The constant c reflects that a derivative loses all information about added constants.

meanings.short: The integral of a function between two limits, a single number: the area under the graph between them, with parts below the axis counted negative.
meanings.long: It is defined as the limit of Riemann sums, and computed as F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F. For a velocity graph it gives the displacement over the time interval.

origin: Latin integrandum, what is to be integrated.

meanings.short: The function being integrated: the f(x) in ∫ f(x) dx.
meanings.long: When the integrand is positive the integral is an area; a change of variable rewrites the integrand and the dx together. Its sign decides whether a piece adds to or subtracts from the integral.

meanings.short: An estimate of an integral: cut the interval into strips, multiply each strip's width by a value of the function in it, and add.
meanings.long: As the strips get narrower the sum approaches the definite integral, which is defined as that limit. Named after Bernhard Riemann.

meanings.short: The theorem that integrating and differentiating undo each other, so a definite integral can be found from any antiderivative.
meanings.long: First form: if F′ = f, then ∫ f from a to b equals F(b) − F(a). Second form: the integral of f from a to x, as a function of x, has derivative f(x).

meanings.short: The variable inside an integral or sum, which could be renamed without changing the result, like the t in ∫ f(t) dt.
meanings.long: When an integral has a variable limit x, a different letter is used inside, so that the two roles do not get mixed up. ∫ f(t) dt and ∫ f(u) du from a to b are the same number.

meanings.short: Finding an integral: adding up very many small pieces, or finding an antiderivative.
meanings.long: It is the reverse of differentiation. Many integrals need a technique, such as substitution, integration by parts or partial fractions; some cannot be written with familiar functions at all.

meanings.short: A tiny change in a variable, such as dx, or the matching change in a function along its tangent line, dy = f′(x) dx.
meanings.long: Leibniz's notation treats dy and dx as tiny amounts that can be multiplied and divided, which makes the chain rule and substitution look natural. dy is the rise along the tangent, close to but not equal to the rise along the curve.

meanings.short: As an adjective: to do with derivatives or with small changes at each point, as in a differential equation.
meanings.long: A differential analysis looks at a small piece and lets it shrink; a differential statement holds at each point, an integral one over a whole region.

meanings.short: A rule for integrating a product of two functions, ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du, which comes from the product rule.
meanings.long: It trades one integral for another that is hopefully easier. It integrates x eˣ, x sin x and ln x, and gives reduction formulas.

meanings.short: A formula that writes an integral containing a power n in terms of the same integral with a lower power, used repeatedly.
meanings.long: For example ∫ (ln x)ⁿ dx = x (ln x)ⁿ − n ∫ (ln x)ⁿ⁻¹ dx, applied until the power reaches zero. Each step lowers the power by one, so a finite number of steps finishes the job.

meanings.short: A change of variable that writes x in terms of a new variable, such as x = sin θ, often to remove a square root.
meanings.long: In ∫ dx/√(1 − x²), putting x = sin θ turns √(1 − x²) into cos θ and dx into cos θ dθ, leaving ∫ dθ. At the end the answer is turned back into the original variable.

meanings.short: Rewriting x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² plus a number, which turns any quadratic into a shifted square.
meanings.long: It solves quadratic equations and prepares integrals such as ∫ dx/(x² + 2x + 5) for a substitution. The added number is chosen so that the square multiplies out to the original x² and x terms.

meanings.short: Splitting a fraction of polynomials into a sum of simpler fractions, each easy to integrate.
meanings.long: For example 1/(x² − 1) = ½/(x − 1) − ½/(x + 1). The method needs the top to have lower degree than the bottom; otherwise long division comes first.

meanings.short: A quick way to find a coefficient in partial fractions: cover one factor of the denominator and put in the x that makes it zero.
meanings.long: For 1/((x − 1)(x + 1)), covering x − 1 and putting x = 1 gives 1/2, the coefficient of 1/(x − 1). It works directly only for factors that are not repeated.

meanings.short: A fraction whose top and bottom are both polynomials, such as (x + 1)/(x² − 4).
meanings.long: Every rational function can be integrated with partial fractions. The answer is built from rational functions, logarithms and arctangents.

meanings.short: Dividing one polynomial by another step by step, like long division of numbers, leaving a polynomial plus a simpler fraction.
meanings.long: It is used when the top of a rational function has degree at least that of the bottom, before partial fractions. For example (x² + 1)/(x − 1) = x + 1 + 2/(x − 1).

meanings.short: A solid made by spinning a flat region about an axis, like a vase shaped on a potter's wheel.
meanings.long: Its volume can be found by slicing it into discs or into cylindrical shells. Both ways give the same answer.

meanings.short: Finding the volume of a solid of revolution by cutting it into thin cylindrical shells around the axis and adding their volumes.
meanings.long: A shell of radius x, height y and thickness dx has volume 2πx y dx, so the volume is the integral of 2πxy dx. It is often easier than slicing into discs when the solid is turned about a vertical axis.

meanings.short: The length of a curve measured along the curve itself, as a piece of string laid along it would show.
meanings.long: Small steps obey ds² = dx² + dy², so for a graph the arc length is the integral of √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx. For a circle of radius r it gives the familiar rθ.

meanings.short: A curve given by writing x and y (and z) as functions of a third variable, the parameter, often thought of as time.
meanings.long: The circle is x = cos t, y = sin t. A parametric curve can loop and cross itself, which a graph y = f(x) cannot.

meanings.short: The path a moving body follows, or more generally the curve traced out by a changing state as time goes on.
meanings.long: A thrown ball's trajectory is a parabola. In the study of differential equations, a trajectory is the path of a solution through the space of possible states.

meanings.short: The integral of a function over an interval divided by the interval's length: the height of a rectangle with the same area.
meanings.long: It is the limit of the ordinary average of many equally spaced samples. The answer depends on the variable you average over.

meanings.short: The value a fluctuating quantity has on average; for a field in the vacuum, its steady background value.
An average in which some values count more: each is multiplied by its weight, and the total divided by the sum of the weights.
meanings.long: The centre of mass is the average position weighted by mass. For a continuous variable the sums become integrals: ∫ x w(x) dx divided by ∫ w(x) dx.

everyday: Normal is just its name; it does not mean that other distributions are abnormal.

meanings.short: The bell-shaped probability curve, highest at the average and falling off equally on both sides; it describes many sums of random effects.
meanings.long: Its formula is proportional to e^(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)), with μ the average and σ the spread. Physicists usually call it the Gaussian distribution.

meanings.short: The function erf(x): the area under a bell curve from 0 to x, scaled so that it tends to 1; it has no simpler formula.
meanings.long: erf(x) = (2/√π) ∫ e^(−t²) dt from 0 to x. It gives the chance that a normally distributed measurement falls within a given distance of the average.

meanings.short: The function Li(x), the integral of 1/ln t from 2 to x, which estimates how many prime numbers there are below x.
meanings.long: It is one of several functions defined by an integral that cannot be written with ordinary functions. It grows a little faster than x / ln x.

meanings.short: Beyond algebra: a transcendental number, such as π or e, solves no polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients; ln x and eˣ are transcendental functions.
meanings.long: A transcendental equation, such as x = e⁻ˣ, mixes such functions with powers and has no algebraic solution; it is solved by graphs or numerical methods. In 18.01 the integral of 1/x is the first place where a transcendental function, ln x, appears.

meanings.short: An integral over an infinite range, or of a function that blows up, defined as a limit of ordinary integrals.
meanings.long: ∫ dx/x² from 1 to ∞ converges to 1, while ∫ dx/x from 1 to ∞ diverges. Whether such an integral is finite depends on how fast the integrand falls off or blows up.

meanings.short: To settle towards a definite finite value: an integral, series or sequence converges when its partial results approach a limit.
meanings.long: The series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … converges to 2. A numerical method converges when its successive answers home in on the true one.

meanings.short: Of people or opinions: to come together on the same view.
To fail to settle on a finite value: a series or integral diverges when its partial results grow without limit or never settle.
meanings.long: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges. In physics a quantity is said to diverge where it becomes infinite, as a density at a point charge or a series beyond its radius of convergence.

meanings.short: To spread out or move apart from one another, as lines leaving a point or paths that start close together.
A sum with infinitely many terms, a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + …, whose value is the limit of its partial sums.
meanings.long: The series converges when the partial sums approach a limit, and diverges otherwise. Only the tail matters for that; if the terms do not shrink to zero the series certainly diverges, and even if they do it may still diverge.

meanings.short: The sum of the first n terms of a series; the series converges if these sums approach a limit as n grows.
meanings.long: For 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + …, the partial sums 1, 1.5, 1.75, … approach 2. Studying them is how one decides whether a series converges.

meanings.short: A series where each term is x times the one before; for x between −1 and 1 the total is 1/(1 − x).
meanings.long: The series diverges for every other x. Many other series are tested by comparing them with a geometric series.

meanings.short: The series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + …, which diverges, though very slowly.
meanings.long: Its partial sums grow like ln n: the first million terms add up to only about 14.4. Comparing it with the integral of 1/x shows that it diverges.

meanings.short: A convergence test: if the ratio of the terms of two positive series tends to a finite, non-zero number, both converge or both diverge.
meanings.long: It lets a complicated series be judged by a simple one with the same behaviour for large n, such as a power of 1/n. For example, the terms of 1/(n² + 1) behave like 1/n², so that series converges.

meanings.short: A series in powers of a variable, a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + …, which behaves like a polynomial with infinitely many terms.
meanings.long: Inside its radius of convergence it can be differentiated and integrated term by term. Many functions, such as eˣ and sin x, can be written as power series.

meanings.short: For a power series, the distance from its centre within which the series converges, and beyond which it diverges.
meanings.long: The geometric series 1 + x + x² + … has radius of convergence 1. For eˣ it is infinite: the series converges for every x.

meanings.short: A power series built from a function's derivatives at one point; its first few terms, a Taylor polynomial, approximate the function near that point.
meanings.long: f(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)(x − a)²/2! + …. Keeping only the first few terms gives the linear and quadratic approximations used throughout physics.

meanings.short: A rule for limits of the form 0/0 or ∞/∞: the limit of f/g equals the limit of f′/g′, if that exists.
meanings.long: It must be used only on a true 0/0 or ∞/∞ form, and sometimes needs to be applied twice. Other forms, such as 0 × ∞ or 1^∞, are first rewritten as a fraction.

meanings.short: A limit that looks like 0/0, ∞/∞, 0 × ∞ or 1^∞, whose value cannot be told from that shape and must be worked out.
meanings.long: sin x / x and 2x / x are both 0/0 at x = 0 but have limits 1 and 2, while x²/x has limit 0. The form alone decides nothing.

meanings.short: A way to estimate an integral by joining neighbouring points of the graph with straight lines and adding the areas of the strips below.
meanings.long: Each strip is a trapezium. The error shrinks as the square of the strip width.

meanings.short: A way to estimate an integral by fitting parabolas through groups of three points; it is far more accurate than straight lines.
meanings.long: The values are weighted 1, 4, 2, 4, …, 4, 1, and the total times the strip width over 3 gives the estimate. It is exact for cubic polynomials, and its error shrinks as the fourth power of the strip width.

origin: Greek parabole, a placing side by side.

meanings.short: The U-shaped curve of y = ax² + bx + c, also the path of a thrown ball when air resistance is ignored.
meanings.long: A parabola is symmetric about a vertical line through its lowest or highest point. Dishes and car headlights are parabolic because a parabola sends parallel rays to a single point, its focus.

meanings.short: Of a partial differential equation: of the diffusion type, first order in time and second order in space.
A function with the same value at x and −x, such as x² or cos x; its graph is mirror-symmetric about the vertical axis.
meanings.long: Its integral from −a to a is twice the integral from 0 to a. Cosine, x² and |x| are all even.

meanings.short: A function that changes sign when x does, f(−x) = −f(x), such as x³ or sin x.
meanings.long: Its graph looks the same after a half turn about the origin, and its integral from −a to a is zero. A sum of odd functions is odd, and an even function times an odd one is odd.

meanings.short: A change, such as a reflection, a rotation or a shift, that leaves something looking exactly the same.
meanings.long: Using symmetry can save work: a symmetric graph needs drawing only on one side. In physics, each continuous symmetry of the laws (shifts in time and space, rotations) brings a conserved quantity (energy, momentum, angular momentum).

meanings.short: Of two quantities: always in the same ratio, so that doubling one doubles the other.
meanings.long: y is proportional to x, written y ∝ x, when y = kx for a fixed number k, the constant of proportionality. 'Inversely proportional' means y = k/x instead.

meanings.short: Having no unit, because the units cancel: a ratio such as v/c is the same number in any system of units.
meanings.long: Formulas are best compared in dimensionless form, and arguments of functions such as eˣ, sin x or ln x must be dimensionless. The fine-structure constant, about 1/137, is a famous dimensionless number.

meanings.short: The whole family of solutions of a differential equation, written with free constants that starting values or boundary conditions then fix.
meanings.long: For dy/dx = −xy it is y = a e^(−x²/2) for any constant a; knowing y(0) = 3 picks a = 3. A second-order equation needs two constants.

meanings.short: A method for finding the largest or smallest value of a function when its variables must satisfy a constraint.
meanings.long: At the best point the gradient of the function is a multiple λ of the gradient of the constraint; λ is the multiplier. In mechanics the multipliers turn out to be the constraint forces.

meanings.short: The point x₀ around which a function is approximated, such as the point where a tangent line touches the curve.
meanings.long: Linear, quadratic and Taylor approximations are accurate near their base point and usually get worse further away. Taylor series are written in powers of x minus the base point.

meanings.short: A value of the input at which a function equals zero, where its graph crosses or touches the horizontal axis; also called a root.
meanings.long: The zeros of x² − 1 are 1 and −1. Newton's method is a way to find zeros numerically.

meanings.short: Entries or terms equal to the number 0, as in a matrix of zeros.
Taking that variable as the one that changes: a derivative with respect to t measures change as t changes, others held fixed.
meanings.long: An integral with respect to x adds up pieces of width dx. The phrase also means relative to, as in a velocity with respect to the ground.

meanings.short: Relative to; measured from the point of view of, as a velocity with respect to the ground.
Without any upper bound: growing larger and larger, past every value.
meanings.long: A quantity that grows without limit is said to diverge or tend to infinity. It never settles towards a finite value.

meanings.short: An operator built from derivatives, such as d/dx or d²/dx² + 1, that turns one function into another.
meanings.long: A differential equation can be written as a differential operator acting on the unknown function. The Laplacian and the d'Alembertian are differential operators in several variables.

meanings.short: A law written as an equation between derivatives at each point, rather than as an integral over a whole region.
meanings.long: Maxwell's equations and conservation laws come in both versions: the integral form speaks about regions and their boundaries, the differential form about each point. The two are linked by the divergence and Stokes theorems.

meanings.short: Rotation in which different parts turn at different rates, as stars nearer a galaxy's centre go round faster than those further out.
meanings.long: A galaxy or the Sun does not turn like a rigid body. Differential rotation shears structures out and shows up in the motions of nearby stars.

meanings.short: The branch of mathematics that studies curved spaces and surfaces with the tools of calculus.
meanings.long: It describes curvature through derivatives of the metric. General relativity is written in its language.

meanings.short: The function that undoes the tangent: arctan x is the angle, between −90 and 90 degrees, whose tangent is x.
meanings.long: Its derivative is 1/(1 + x²), so it appears in integrals of that form. Finding the direction of a vector from its components uses it, with care over which quarter of the plane the vector lies in.
